05-1.title: RAG pipeline end to end
05-1.tldr: Two halves — ingestion (parse → chunk → embed → index) and query (embed → retrieve → rerank → assemble → generate); every stage is separable and can fail.
points: Ingestion: parse files, chunk, embed, and write vectors to the store.
Query: embed the query, retrieve top-k (dense and/or sparse), rerank, assemble context.
Generation sees only the assembled context; cite from it.
Quality drops can come from any stage — isolate them.

05-2.title: Pipeline stages
05-2.tldr: The same pipeline stage by stage: query embedding → vector search → context assembly → prompt construction → generation.
points: Embed the query with the same model used for the index.
Vector search returns top-k candidate chunks.
Assemble the hits into a context string and build the prompt.
Generate the answer from that context.

05-3.title: Measuring retrieval
05-3.tldr: Use a labeled (query, relevant docs) set and ranked metrics — Recall@k, Precision@k, MRR, NDCG — and track zero-result rate.
points: Recall@k: did the relevant docs make the top-k?
Precision@k / MRR / NDCG: how high and how well-ordered the hits are.
Track zero-result rate and score distributions in production.
Judge retrieval separately from generation.

05-4.title: Modular RAG
05-4.tldr: Simple RAG is a fixed chain; Modular RAG decomposes it into swappable modules (indexing, retrieval, fusion, reranking, query rewriting, generation) that can be routed and scheduled.
points: Simple RAG: retrieve → stuff → generate, fixed order.
Modular RAG: interchangeable modules with routing/orchestration.
Lets you add rewriting, reranking, or iteration per query.

05-5.title: Choosing chunk size
05-5.tldr: Too small loses context and splits answers; too large dilutes the embedding. Start at a few hundred tokens with modest overlap.
points: Small chunks: precise but may lack context or split the answer.
Large chunks: richer context but a diluted, multi-topic embedding.
Start ~a few hundred tokens with small overlap; tune by measuring.

05-6.title: Chunks too small or too large
05-6.tldr: Too small: the answer splits and the answer-bearing chunk can be missed. Too large: the embedding blends topics, precision drops, and prompt cost rises.
points: Small: context lost, answer split, more index overhead.
Large: embedding averages topics, precision down, prompt budget wasted.
The code guards mechanics (invalid values, limits), not retrieval quality.

05-7.title: Fixed-size vs semantic chunking
05-7.tldr: Fixed-size is cheap and deterministic but cuts mid-sentence; structure/sentence-aware chunking keeps chunks coherent at the cost of variable size and extra processing.
points: Fixed-size: deterministic and cheap, but fragments mid-sentence/mid-table.
Semantic/structure-aware: split on real boundaries; coherent, variable size.
Best: sentence/structure-aware with a cap, not raw character windows.

05-8.title: Chunk overlap
05-8.tldr: A small overlap preserves meaning across a boundary; too much duplicates content, inflates the index, and returns near-identical hits.
points: Overlap keeps boundary-spanning answers retrievable.
Too much overlap duplicates text and crowds out diverse hits.
Non-overlapping is cheaper but risks losing the boundary fact.

05-9.title: Chunking tables, code, headings
05-9.tldr: Capture structure at parse time and carry it as metadata — keep tables intact (row/column), preserve code boundaries, and split on headings.
points: Preserve structure at parse time, not chunk time.
Tables: keep rows/columns whole or serialize per record.
Code: split on function/class boundaries and keep fences.
Headings: use them as split boundaries.

05-10.title: Answer cut across chunks
05-10.tldr: If the answer spans a boundary, the retrieved chunk holds only half of it. Fix with overlap, sentence/structure-aware splitting, and neighbor expansion at serve time.
points: Boundary cuts produce half-answers that still rank.
Overlap + sentence/structure-aware chunking reduce it.
At serve time, expand a hit with its neighbors.

05-11.title: Choosing an embedding model
05-11.tldr: Bigger isn't automatically better: fit to domain and language, use the right query/passage prefixes, pick an affordable dimension, and weigh latency/cost.
points: Domain + language fit beats raw size.
Asymmetric models need correct query/passage prefixes.
Dimension drives storage/latency; a smaller in-domain model can win.
Evaluate recall on your data, not a leaderboard.

05-12.title: Same embedding model for query & docs
05-12.tldr: Yes — both sides must use the same model, and asymmetric models need the correct role prefix on each side, or the vectors aren't comparable.
points: One model embeds both queries and documents.
Asymmetric models: apply query vs passage prefixes.
Mixing models or dropping prefixes degrades retrieval.

05-13.title: Re-embedding after model swap
05-13.tldr: Stored vectors belong to one model; a new model — even at the same dimension — is a different space, so every chunk must be re-embedded and the index rebuilt.
points: Vectors from different models aren't comparable.
Same dimension does not mean same space.
Re-embed the whole corpus and rebuild the index.

05-14.title: Multilingual retrieval
05-14.tldr: Use a multilingual/alignment embedding so queries and docs share one space; otherwise translate at index or query time and store language metadata.
points: Prefer a multilingual/alignment embedding model.
Otherwise translate at index or query time.
Store language metadata to route and evaluate per language.

05-15.title: Dense vs sparse + rank fusion
05-15.tldr: Dense matches meaning but can miss rare exact terms; sparse (BM25) matches literal terms but fails on paraphrase; fuse both with reciprocal rank fusion.
points: Dense: embeddings, semantic match; weak on exact tokens.
Sparse/BM25: literal term match; weak on paraphrase.
Fuse with RRF: combine ranks, not raw scores.
Weighting is often ignored in favor of RRF.

05-16.title: When keyword search wins
05-16.tldr: Keyword wins on exact identifiers, codes, rare names, jargon, and small/distinctive corpora; dense wins on paraphrase and intent. Best is hybrid.
points: Exact codes/IDs/names favor keyword.
Paraphrase/intent favor dense.
Combine both to cover each other's blind spots.

05-17.title: Semantic misses exact codes
05-17.tldr: Opaque tokens (codes, SKUs, UUIDs, rare names) carry little semantic signal, so a semantically close but wrong chunk can outrank the exact hit — and dense results are rarely empty, so no fallback fires.
points: Short opaque tokens embed to near-random neighbors.
A wrong-but-close chunk can rank above the exact hit.
Fix: metadata/exact filtering, a sparse leg, or an exact-match boost.

05-18.title: Retrieve 5 vs 20
05-18.tldr: Higher k raises recall but costs tokens/latency and can dilute; lower k is precise and cheap. Retrieve more then rerank down when you have a reranker.
points: More docs → recall up, tokens/latency up.
Fewer docs → precision, lower cost.
Ideal: retrieve many, rerank to few (needs a wired reranker).

05-19.title: SQL + documents retrieval
05-19.tldr: Keep paths explicit: route structured questions to a schema-aware text-to-SQL/table tool and unstructured to document retrieval, then merge and ground results.
points: Structured → text-to-SQL/table query (validatable).
Unstructured → document retrieval.
Merge and ground; don't flatten tables into text.

05-20.title: What reranking adds
05-20.tldr: First-stage retrieval optimizes recall with cheap approximate similarity; a cross-encoder reranker scores candidates jointly with the query to reorder the top-k for precision — but only over candidates retrieval already returned.
points: Retrieval: recall, cheap, approximate.
Rerank: precision, joint query+doc scoring, expensive.
Cannot recover what retrieval never returned.

05-21.title: Is the reranker helping?
05-21.tldr: You can't tell from order alone; on a labeled set, compare ranking metrics (NDCG/MRR/precision) with and without the reranker on the same candidates.
points: Order alone isn't evidence.
Compare ranked metrics on the same candidate set.
If NDCG doesn't improve, it's just reordering.

05-22.title: Rerank every query?
05-22.tldr: Rerank only when it pays off: high-stakes or ambiguous queries with low first-stage precision and a bounded candidate count; skip exact lookups and latency-critical cheap queries.
points: Rerank when precision matters and candidates are bounded.
Skip exact-match, high-volume, latency-critical queries.
Decide per query, not globally.

05-23.title: Reranking latency
05-23.tldr: Latency scales with candidate count and batching: a cross-encoder over ~50–100 candidates adds tens to low-hundreds of ms; an LLM-judge reranker is one call per document (O(N)).
points: Cross-encoder: one batched call over N candidates.
LLM-judge: one call per doc — much slower.
Weigh added latency against precision gain.

05-24.title: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder
05-24.tldr: Bi-encoders embed query and document independently (fast, precomputable, indexable); cross-encoders feed query+document together for a precise relevance score (slow, per-pair).
points: Bi-encoder: independent embeddings, scalable retrieval.
Cross-encoder: joint scoring, higher precision, per-pair cost.
Use bi-encoder to retrieve, cross-encoder to rerank.

05-25.title: Query rewriting vs expansion
05-25.tldr: Rewriting makes a query self-contained (coreference, typos, prior-turn reliance); expansion adds terms/synonyms or a hypothetical answer (HyDE) to bridge vocabulary gaps.
points: Rewriting: coreference/ellipsis, typos, drop turn dependence.
Expansion: synonyms or a hypothetical answer (HyDE).
Rewriting for multi-turn/malformed; expansion for vocabulary mismatch.

05-26.title: Handling vague queries
05-26.tldr: Detect ambiguity and either ask a clarifying question or rewrite to the most likely intent; cheap path is a rewrite, interactive path is a clarification turn.
points: Rewrite resolves coreference/ellipsis for free.
Ask a clarification only when it changes the retrieval target.
Don't blindly retrieve on an ambiguous query.

05-27.title: Decomposing multi-part questions
05-27.tldr: Split a compound question into independently answerable sub-questions, retrieve for each (often in parallel), then synthesize.
points: Break 'compare A and B on X and Y' into sub-questions.
Retrieve per sub-question; merge and dedupe.
Synthesize across the sub-answers.

05-28.title: Multi-hop retrieval
05-28.tldr: Multi-hop runs more than one retrieval step, using the first hop's result to form the next query, because the answer needs a bridging entity not present in the original question.
points: The answer needs a bridging entity/fact.
Each hop feeds the next query.
Single-pass fails when the link isn't in the query.

05-29.title: Multi-document questions
05-29.tldr: Retrieve a candidate set per sub-query or entity, merge and deduplicate, and let the generator synthesize across them (or add an aggregation step).
points: Per-sub-query retrieval, then merge/dedupe.
Ranked-list fusion across queries.
Generator synthesizes across documents.

05-30.title: When to skip RAG
05-30.tldr: Skip retrieval for general knowledge the model already holds, when latency/cost matter and the corpus won't add signal, or for conversational turns — but you need a way to decide.
points: Skip for general knowledge, reasoning, or code the model knows.
Skip when the corpus adds no signal and cost/latency matter.
Decide with a classifier or a sufficiency check.

05-31.title: Chunk doesn't contain the answer
05-31.tldr: 'Looked relevant' isn't 'contains the answer': read the chunk and confirm the answer span is present; if not, retrieval failed; if yes, generation failed.
points: First check: is the answer actually in the retrieved chunk?
No → retrieval failure (chunking, index, query mismatch).
Yes → generation/grounding failure.

05-32.title: Context doesn't answer the question
05-32.tldr: Detect that the context is insufficient, then answer only from what's supported: gate on retrieval score/answerability, allow explicit 'I don't know', and verify claims against the context.
points: Detect insufficient context (score/answerability gate).
Allow explicit abstention ('I don't know').
Ground/verify claims against the context.

05-33.title: Conflicting / outdated documents
05-33.tldr: Apply precedence before generation — recency, source authority, or an explicit priority field; dedupe/reconcile; and surface the conflict (or abstain).
points: Precedence: newest / most authoritative / priority field.
Dedupe and reconcile conflicting facts.
Surface the conflict or abstain rather than guess.

05-34.title: No relevant documents
05-34.tldr: When retrieval returns nothing relevant, abstain rather than answer from noise: gate on a score threshold or answerability check and return 'not enough information'.
points: Gate on retrieval score or answerability.
Abstain or ask a clarifying question.
Don't generate from out-of-scope chunks.

05-35.title: Different answers on different days
05-35.tldr: Run-to-run variation comes from sampling (temperature/seed), non-deterministic remote rerankers, and embedding drift (provider updates the model behind the same name, or you switch models).
points: Sampling: pin temperature 0 and use a seed.
Remote rerankers may be non-deterministic.
Embedding drift: fingerprint the model and re-index on change.

05-36.title: Vocabulary mismatch
05-36.tldr: The doc says 'myocardial infarction', the user says 'heart attack': use semantic embeddings, query expansion/synonyms, HyDE, and hybrid search to bridge the wording gap.
points: Semantic embeddings match paraphrases.
Query expansion / synonyms.
HyDE: retrieve with a generated hypothetical answer.
Hybrid search catches exact terms.

05-37.title: Per-stage error handling
05-37.tldr: Isolate each stage so one failure degrades rather than aborts: retrieval returns empty/flagged, reranking falls back to pre-rerank order, generation surfaces a structured error.
points: Typed errors per stage.
Explicit fallbacks (empty result, pre-rerank order).
Degrade, don't abort the whole pipeline.

05-38.title: Cutting tokens without losing quality
05-38.tldr: Retrieve fewer but better chunks (rerank a larger candidate set down to small k), summarize long chunks, and trim history.
points: Retrieve many, rerank to few (needs a reranker).
Summarize long chunks before insertion.
Trim conversation history.

05-39.title: Building a retrieval eval set
05-39.tldr: Bootstrap with real queries from logs, then label relevance with an LLM judge, RAGAS-style (a strong model's cited chunks as gold), or synthetic queries built from known documents.
points: Mine real queries from logs.
Label via LLM judge or a strong model's citations.
Or synthesize queries from known documents (doc = gold).

05-40.title: Multiple document formats
05-40.tldr: Normalize everything to one record shape (text + metadata + id) at ingestion, with a parser per format behind a registry keyed by type, preserving format-specific structure as metadata.
points: One record shape: text + metadata + id.
Parser per format behind a registry.
Keep format-specific structure as metadata.

05-41.title: RAG vs pasting a long context
05-41.tldr: Pasting whole documents is simpler and avoids chunking errors but is expensive, slow, and noisy; retrieval pays a one-time chunking/index cost and sends only relevant, citable chunks.
points: Paste: simple, no chunking bugs, but costly/slow/noisy.
RAG: cheaper per call, citable, scales past the window.
Choose by cost, latency, and need to cite.
